newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Trade slows amid forex jitters.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Trade slows amid forex jitters.

text.p: Asian debt markets remained quiet on Friday as bankers continued to cast a nervous eye toward Southeast Asia generally and Thailand in particular.
The currency turmoil that had spilled over from the Thai baht into other Southeast Asian currencies settled down on Friday as central banks appeared to take the upper hand.
But debt traders said they remained cautious.
"It seems that the Thai government has taken control and that there is little risk of a baht devaluation," said a debt syndicate manager in Hong Kong responsible for Thai issues.
"But we're taking a wait-and-see approach and won't be calling our clients until next week," he said.
The Thai baht stabilized in quiet late trade on Friday after the Bank of Thailand asked local banks to stop quoting transactions with offshore players.
The baht was trading at 25.775/25.875 to the U.S. dollar in late trade versus 25.450/25.650 this morning.
"The market was almost silent today as we did not have transactions with offshore players," a dealer at a foreign bank told Reuters in Bangkok.
Debt traders in Hong Kong said spreads for Asian issues widened overnight in overseas markets.
"Most of the Asian names in the U.S. widened out by five to 10 basis points," said a capital markets manager.
"But that is to be expected because investors overseas tend to be more nervous about what happens in Asia than Asian investors would be," he added.
Guangdong Enterprises placed a 144a bond into U.S. markets overnight via lead manager Merrill Lynch.
Bankers said the 10-year paper should help the company with its cash flow.
The US$500 million notes are due in 2007. They pay a semi-annual coupon of 8.875 percent and were priced to yield 8.89 percent, or 223 basis points over comparable Treasuries.
Debt traders in Hong Kong did not quibble with the pricing, with some even calling it generous. But many called the deal "difficult," mostly because of its split rating.
Moody's Investors Service on Friday upgraded the senior unsecured rating of Hong Kong-based Guangdong Enterprises to Baa3 from Ba1.
Moody's said the rating reflected the Guangdong provincial government's decision to issue a letter of support for the company.

But Standard and Poor's affirmed the company's rating at BB. And while S&P said the rating reflected the relationship and support of the Guangdong government, it cautioned that it did not believe the support was iron-clad.

In a conference call held today to discuss the recent upgrades of China and Hong Kong, S&P's managing director Paul Coughlin said that the support Guangdong Enterprises enjoys is materially different from the backing Guangdong provides for investment institutions such as Guangdong International Trust and Investment (GITIC).
"There is a clear expectation from the central government down that the government of Guangdong Province will stand behind GITIC," said Coughlin.

But it is also "quite clear there are strong reservations about the moral responsibility or the policy wisdom of extending this support to companies that operate outside the borders of the People's Republic and this does include Hong Kong-based companies," he said.
S&P also said in its conference call that it does not expect to rerate China for several years because more time is needed to assess Beijing's progress in implementing financial reforms.
S&P on Wednesday raised China's sovereign debt rating to BBB-plus from BBB. It also raised Hong Kong's foreign currency rating to A-plus from Single-A.
